summary: Capacity provisioned for the first Run is still there when the second arrives, because an enrolled node agent holds the host runtime open. The second Run reuses that machine and its layers instead of provisioning a second one. The listing names the machine it becomes and states what its provider negotiated over it: this one stops and resumes a machine under one identity, keeps its disk while it is stopped, deduplicates a repeated provision on the operation key, and can list what Mercator owns there. The first Run is what makes any of that possible, and its disposition says so: it releases its workload rather than terminating its host, because the machine it built is a lease with its own lifecycle and a Run ending is not that lease ending. A first Run that terminated would leave the second one nothing to find, whatever the listing negotiated. Mercator does all of this today on a node an operator enrolled by hand. What is missing is the provisioned-to-enrolled transition, twice over: a fresh machine arriving with an agent that opens a session, and a host keeping what its workload fetched, so the second Run finds warm layers rather than a cold pull. The second Run's own disposition is deliberately no longer the evidence of reuse: both lanes of that Run release now, so what says it reused the machine is the reason, the candidate disposition, and the two stages costing nothing.
